original_value:
Textual deception constitutes a major problem for online security. Many studies have argued that deceptiveness leaves traces in writing style, which could be detected using text classification techniques. By conducting an extensive literature review of existing empirical work, we demonstrate that while certain linguistic features have been indicative of deception in certain corpora, they fail to generalize across divergent semantic domains. We suggest that deceptiveness as such leaves no
            content-invariant stylistic trace
            , and textual similarity measures provide a superior means of classifying texts as potentially deceptive. Additionally, we discuss forms of deception beyond semantic content, focusing on hiding author identity by
            writing style obfuscation
            . Surveying the literature on both author identification and obfuscation techniques, we conclude that current style transformation methods fail to achieve reliable obfuscation while simultaneously ensuring semantic faithfulness to the original text. We propose that future work in style transformation should pay particular attention to disallowing semantically drastic changes.

result.paraphrase: Textual deception poses a major challenge for online security. Many studies have claimed that deception leaves stylistic traces in writing that can be detected with text classification methods. Through an extensive review of empirical research, we show that although certain linguistic features indicate deception in some corpora, they do not generalize across different semantic domains. We argue that deceptiveness itself leaves no content-invariant stylistic trace, and that text similarity measures are a better way to classify texts as potentially deceptive. We also examine deception beyond semantic content, with particular attention to concealing author identity through writing style obfuscation. Reviewing the literature on author identification and obfuscation techniques, we conclude that current style transformation methods do not reliably obfuscate while also preserving semantic fidelity to the original text. We suggest that future style transformation research should explicitly prevent semantically drastic changes.
